blocks.text: The official account follows visits to Serbian churches, the ordering of monastic life on Athonite and Palestinian models, and the appointment of Arsenius as successor. Its narrative connects pastoral organization with mediation among rulers and further journeys to the Holy Land. It then locates his relics at Mileševa and describes their veneration after the return from Bulgaria.

blocks.text: His son, Saint Sava, organised the Christian Church wonderfully, and wonderfully he inspired the educational and scholarly work in the state created by his father. This Saint Sava, the Archbishop of Serbia, after he had travelled all over Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria, preaching the Gospel of the Son of God, died in Bulgaria. His body was trans- ferred to and buried in a monastery in Herze- govina. Afterwards, in times of national hard- ships and slavery, great pilgrimages took place to the grave of the Saint, which became the comforting and inspiring centre for the oppressed nation; the Turks destroyed the tomb, carried the body over to Belgrade and burnt it, in order to lessen the Serbian national and religious enthusiasm. The result was just the contrary.
blocks.locator: LectureII, For Cross and Freedom, pp26–27, paragraph about Saint Sava

blocks.context: Nikolai Velimirovic’s 1916 Serbian Orthodox lecture; the historical language and contemporary national setting are those of the printed source.

blocks.text: Saint Sava’s belief was the same as the belief of Saint Patrick and Saint Augustine. His hopes were the same as theirs too. He believed in the one saving Gospel of Christ, as they did. He hoped men could be educated by this divine Gospel, to be heroic in suffering and pure and holy in the enjoyments of life, just as the great saints of this island doubtless hoped and worked.
